title: Titus Andronicus
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Rome and the forest outside it, over a few days
lengthNote: About 2,500 lines, nearly all verse. Act I is a single scene of some 495 lines, played without a break.
openingLine: Noble patricians, patrons of my right
summary: Titus comes home from ten years of war against the Goths with four surviving sons, two in coffins, and a captive queen. Before the funeral is over he has Tamora's eldest boy hacked apart and burned on the family tomb, and every horror in the next four acts answers that one decision. Tamora marries the new emperor, her sons kill Lavinia's husband and cut out her tongue and hands, Titus loses a hand and two more sons to a trick, and the play ends with a queen eating her children at dinner. It is Shakespeare's first tragedy and his most extreme.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: Every quotation here is checked word for word against this text, and act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, which modern editions vary from by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Early, and possibly the earliest of the tragedies. Ben Jonson's 1614 joke about the play's admirers implies a first audience around 1589.

atAGlance.label: First staged
atAGlance.note: Philip Henslowe entered a performance of Titus & ondronicus at the Rose in his account book.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: John Danter's quarto for Edward White and Thomas Millington, the first printing of any Shakespeare play. One copy survives, in the Folger.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Ovid's Philomela, Seneca's Thyestes, the Lucrece story and a mass of Roman material, combined by Shakespeare himself.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I is one unbroken scene; the Folio adds the fly scene at 3.2, which no quarto prints.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A funeral, an election and a sacrifice
structure.summary: Everything is set in motion in a single unbroken scene of nearly five hundred lines. Two brothers fight over the empire, the people offer it to Titus, and Titus hands it to Saturninus. Between those decisions he burns Tamora's eldest son on his family tomb, stabs his own son Mutius for blocking a doorway, and watches the woman he has just wronged crowned Empress of Rome. By the end of the act every later murder has a cause.

scenes.title: Before the Capitol
scenes.summary: Titus returns with his dead sons and his prisoners, sacrifices Alarbus, refuses the empire, gives it to Saturninus, kills Mutius in a quarrel over Lavinia, and looks on while Saturninus marries Tamora instead.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The hunt, the pit and the forest
structure.summary: The court rides out to hunt and the play moves into the woods, where Aaron has buried a bag of gold and written a letter that will hang two innocent men. Bassianus is stabbed and dropped into a pit, Titus's sons Quintus and Martius fall in after him and are arrested for the murder, and Lavinia is taken away by Chiron and Demetrius. Marcus finds her at the end, and cannot say what he sees.

scenes.title: Aaron and the brothers
scenes.summary: Aaron stops Chiron and Demetrius fighting over Lavinia and tells them to take her together during the hunt, in woods he calls ruthless, dreadful, deaf and dull.

scenes.title: The hunt is up
scenes.summary: Horns, hounds and morning greetings. Demetrius ends the scene telling his brother which doe they are actually hunting.

scenes.title: The pit
scenes.summary: Bassianus is murdered and Lavinia dragged off; Aaron leads Quintus and Martius to the pit where the body lies and fetches the emperor to find them standing over it.

scenes.title: Marcus finds Lavinia
scenes.summary: Chiron and Demetrius leave her mutilated and jeering at her to write down who did it. Marcus, alone with her, talks for forty lines about Philomela, lutes and rivers.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The hand, and the fly
structure.summary: Titus pleads for his condemned sons to a street that has already emptied, then lies down and tells his griefs to the stones. Aaron arrives with the emperor's offer: a hand for two lives. Titus lets him cut it off and gets back two heads and his own hand in scorn. He stops weeping, laughs, and takes his vow. The act closes on a family dinner and a killed fly.

scenes.title: A hand for two heads
scenes.summary: Titus pleads, loses the argument to an empty street, gives his hand to Aaron, receives his sons' heads, laughs, and swears revenge; Lucius is banished and goes to raise an army among the Goths.

scenes.title: The fly
scenes.summary: At a banquet Titus reads Lavinia's signs aloud, then attacks Marcus for killing a fly, and forgives him once Marcus says the fly looked like the empress's Moor.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Names in the sand, a black child, arrows to the gods
structure.summary: Lavinia chases her nephew for his copy of Ovid, turns to the story of Philomela, and writes her attackers' names in the sand with a staff held in her mouth. Tamora's child is born black and Aaron kills the nurse to keep it. Titus, apparently mad, shoots petitions to the gods over the palace wall, and in secret begins to arrange what he intends to do.

scenes.title: Ovid and the staff
scenes.summary: Lavinia finds the tale of Tereus in the Metamorphoses, then writes Stuprum and two names in the sand. Marcus swears the family to revenge; Titus tells him the dam will wake.

scenes.title: Aaron and his son
scenes.summary: The nurse brings Tamora's black baby with orders to kill it. Aaron kills her instead, refuses his accomplices, and carries the child away to raise among the Goths.

scenes.title: The arrows
scenes.summary: Titus sends his kinsmen to dig for Justice in the underworld and to fish for her at sea, then has them shoot letters addressed to the gods into the emperor's court.

scenes.title: Saturninus reads
scenes.summary: The emperor rages over the arrows and orders the Clown who delivered a letter to be hanged. Tamora calms him and goes off to play Revenge at Titus's house.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Revenge comes to dinner
structure.summary: Lucius returns at the head of a Gothic army, takes Aaron prisoner, and buys a full confession with a promise to keep the baby alive. Tamora arrives at Titus's study disguised as Revenge and leaves her sons behind as hostages to his madness. He cuts their throats, bakes them, serves them to their mother, kills Lavinia and then Tamora, and the survivors count what is left of Rome.

scenes.title: Aaron on the ladder
scenes.summary: Caught with the child, Aaron trades the whole plot for the baby's life and then lists his crimes with relish, wishing only that he had done ten thousand more.

scenes.title: Revenge, Rape and Murder
scenes.summary: Tamora comes disguised to Titus's study; he plays along, keeps Chiron and Demetrius when she goes, binds them, and cuts their throats over a basin Lavinia holds between her stumps.

scenes.title: The banquet
scenes.summary: Titus serves the pie, kills Lavinia, names the pie's contents, stabs Tamora and is killed by Saturninus, who is killed by Lucius. Lucius is made emperor, sentences Aaron to be buried alive, and orders Tamora thrown to the birds.

characters.name: Titus Andronicus
characters.role: Roman general, back from ten years of war
characters.summary: He has buried twenty-one sons for Rome and cannot imagine an argument that Rome's forms will not settle. He gives away the empire, sacrifices a prisoner because the rite requires it, and kills his own son for standing in a doorway. When the forms stop working he goes to the stones, then to the gods by arrow, and finally does the arithmetic himself with a knife and a pie dish.
characters.clue: Refuses the empire, then kills his own son for blocking a door, and ends the play dressed as a cook.

relationships.label: burns her son, then feeds her the others
hands the empire to, and is ruined by

characters.name: Lavinia
characters.summary: She is bargained over by two men in the first scene and has her tongue and hands cut off in the second act so that she can name nobody. What follows is the hardest thing in Shakespeare to stage: forty lines in which her uncle describes her, scene after scene in which her family guesses at her meaning, and then the moment she takes a staff in her mouth and writes two names in the sand.
characters.clue: Writes the names of her attackers in sand with a staff held in her mouth, guided by her stumps.

relationships.label: niece of, and read aloud by

characters.name: Tamora
characters.role: Queen of the Goths, then Empress of Rome
characters.summary: She begins the play kneeling in the street to beg for her son's life and is refused in the name of piety. Within two hundred lines she is empress, and she spends the rest of the play making Rome pay. The play lets her be right about the sacrifice and monstrous about everything after it, and she never pretends the two are connected by anything but appetite.
characters.clue: Kneels in the street for her eldest son's life, is refused, and is crowned empress in the same scene.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.role: A Moor, Tamora's lover, and the engineer of the plot
characters.summary: He buries the gold, writes the letter, guides the brothers to the pit, talks Titus out of his hand and watches through a crack in the wall while the heads come back. He is also the only parent in the play who protects a child: when his black son is born he kills the nurse, refuses the empress and carries the baby off. On the ladder he confesses everything and regrets one good deed.
characters.clue: Laughs until his own eyes are wet at the sight of Titus getting two heads back for his hand, then risks everything for his newborn son.

relationships.label: takes his hand by a trick

characters.name: Saturninus
characters.role: The late emperor's elder son, and Rome's new emperor
characters.summary: He is given the empire by the man he immediately insults, and loses Lavinia to his brother within a hundred lines of claiming her. Everything he does afterwards is reaction: he marries Tamora on the spot, condemns Titus's sons on evidence Aaron arranged for him, orders a clown hanged for carrying a letter, and dies at his own banquet without ever understanding who was moving him.
characters.clue: Chooses a new bride mid-scene when the first one is carried off, and never asks who arranged the evidence he sentences men on.

relationships.label: owes the empire to, and turns on

characters.name: Lucius
characters.role: Titus's eldest surviving son, exile, and the last emperor standing
characters.summary: He asks for the sacrifice in the first scene, which makes him the cause of the revenge as much as his father. Banished for trying to rescue his brothers, he comes back at the head of the army of the people whose prince he had burned. He swears by a god Aaron does not believe in to keep a baby alive, and keeps the promise while sentencing its father to starve in the ground.
characters.clue: Calls for the sacrifice in Act I, then returns with a Gothic army to avenge what it caused.

characters.name: Marcus Andronicus
characters.role: Tribune of the People, and Titus's brother
characters.summary: He offers Rome to Titus, argues him into burying Mutius, and finds Lavinia in the wood. His long speech over her has been the play's most argued-about passage for two centuries: it is beautiful, it is about Ovid, and it does nothing for her. He kills the fly, thinks of the staff in the sand, and is left at the end trying to talk a city back into one piece.
characters.clue: Speaks forty lines of elegant verse to a niece who cannot answer, and later kills a fly at dinner.

characters.name: Demetrius
characters.summary: He and his brother open Act II with swords drawn over Lavinia and are still finishing each other's sentences when Titus cuts their throats. Demetrius supplies the reasoning: she is a woman, therefore may be won; she is Lavinia, therefore must be loved. He puts the first knife into Bassianus, talks Tamora out of killing Lavinia on the spot — thrash the corn first, burn the straw after — and jeers at her to go and tell.
characters.clue: Tells his brother that more water goes by the mill than the miller knows of, and strikes Bassianus first.

characters.name: Chiron
characters.summary: The younger and touchier of the pair, mocked by his brother for the dancing-rapier their mother gave him in the quarrel that opens Act II. He orders Bassianus's body dragged to a secret hole, then tells Lavinia to write her meaning down if her stumps will let her, a joke the play turns into the instrument of his death. Watching Alarbus led away in 1.1, he says Scythia was never half so barbarous, and he is not counting himself.
characters.clue: Jeers that Lavinia should write with her stumps, and is bound and bled over a basin she holds.

characters.name: Young Lucius
characters.summary: He carries the books his aunt chases him for, and his copy of Ovid is what lets the family finally learn who attacked her. He offers to stab Chiron and Demetrius with a dagger and is told there is a better way. At the end he cannot get a word out for crying, which in this play is the only honest response anyone manages to the sight of the dead.
characters.clue: Drops his schoolbooks running from his aunt, and one of them is the Metamorphoses.

relationships.label: nephew of, and unwitting help to

themes.name: Revenge as a working system
themes.summary: Nobody in the play invents revenge; they all inherit it. Alarbus dies because Lucius asks for a sacrifice, Bassianus dies because Tamora was refused, Chiron and Demetrius die because Lavinia was attacked, and Tamora dies at a table. Each killing is presented by its author as the settling of an account, which is why the play can keep going after the point at which grief should have stopped it.
themes.development: The sacrifice at 1.1 sets the rate; Tamora's aside at 1.1.451 promises a day; Titus takes his vow over two severed heads in 3.1; and 5.3 collects everything owed in nine lines.

themes.name: Law, and what is left when it goes
themes.summary: Rome has elections, tribunes, judges and a senate, and every one of them fails inside two acts. Titus pleads in a street the tribunes have already left, then tells his sorrows to the stones because stones at least do not interrupt. By Act IV he is digging for Justice in the underworld and shooting petitions to the gods over the palace wall.
themes.development: The election in 1.1 is the last working civic act; the trial of Quintus and Martius happens offstage on planted evidence; 3.1 has Titus pleading to nobody; 4.3 sends letters to Jove because there is nowhere else to send them.

themes.name: Proof, and who arranged it
themes.summary: Rome keeps convicting on objects. A bag of gold under a tree and a letter dropped where it will be found are enough to condemn two men for a murder they did not commit. The one piece of true testimony in the play has to be written in sand with a staff held in a mouth, and even then Marcus has to swear the family to believe it.
themes.development: Aaron buries the gold and writes the letter in 2.3; the pit makes two innocent men look like murderers on sight; Lavinia writes Stuprum and two names at 4.1.79; Aaron confirms all of it from a ladder in 5.1.

themes.name: Lavinia without a tongue
themes.summary: The play cuts out its heroine's tongue at the end of Act II and then spends three acts on the problem of what she still means. Her family talk at her, over her and for her. Titus claims he can read every sign she makes and promises to wrest an alphabet out of her stumps, which is devotion and also another way of speaking on her behalf.
themes.development: She argues fluently with Tamora at 2.3; Marcus describes her for forty lines at 2.4; Titus interprets her at 3.2; she writes for herself at 4.1, and her father kills her at 5.3 without asking.

themes.name: Aaron, and the language Rome uses
themes.summary: Everyone in Rome describes Aaron by his colour, and so does he. The difference is that he makes an argument of it: coal-black scorns to take another hue, while a white face betrays its owner by blushing. When his son is born he will not let the baby be called a devil, and the scene gives him the only unconditional love anyone in the play shows a child.
themes.development: He is a silent prisoner through 1.1; he walks out of 3.1 with a hand he has just cut off and a couplet rhyming his soul to his face; 4.2 has him defending the baby against its own mother and brothers; 5.3 sentences him to be buried breast-deep and starved.

themes.name: Rites, and what they are worth
themes.summary: Titus does nothing in Act I that Rome would call wrong. He buries his sons with the proper rite, refuses the empire out of modesty, offers the sacrifice the dead are owed, and kills Mutius for dishonouring the family. The play then follows each of those correct acts to its consequence, and leaves the audience wondering whether ceremony was ever doing the work everyone believed it was doing.
themes.development: The tomb opens at 1.1 and Alarbus burns; Mutius is refused burial and then granted it after a scene of kneeling; the final act distributes burial as a verdict, with Tamora thrown to the birds.

themes.name: Hands, tongues and writing
themes.summary: The play is obsessed with the body parts that make meaning. Hands are cut off, bargained for, sent back in scorn, carried between teeth and used to write in sand. Tongues are cut out, bitten, and wished away. When Marcus says the word hands at dinner, Titus cannot stop talking about it, and nor can the play.
themes.development: Lavinia loses both at 2.4; Titus gives his away at 3.1 and gets it back with two heads; in 3.2 the word hands becomes a wound; in 4.1 a staff stands in for the hand and sand for the tongue.

techniques.name: Objects that carry the plot
techniques.definition: A physical thing on stage doing work that speech would otherwise have to do.
techniques.inThisBook: A bag of gold, a letter, a book of Ovid, a staff, a basin, a severed hand, two heads and a pie. The play moves from one object to the next, and an audience always knows exactly what is being carried on and what it will cost.

techniques.name: Classical allusion
techniques.definition: Naming a Greek or Roman story so that it explains, or supplies a pattern for, the action on stage.
techniques.inThisBook: Philomela is not decoration here. Lavinia turns the pages of the Metamorphoses to the tale of Tereus because it is the nearest thing she has to a sentence, and Titus tops it at 5.2: worse than Philomel, and worse than Procne in return.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Two opposed terms set against each other inside a single line or sentence.
techniques.inThisBook: Roman against barbarous, fair against black, white-limed walls against coal-black. The play thinks in pairs, and Aaron handles the figure better than anyone in Rome, because the pairs are the ones the city has used to place him and he turns each of them over.

techniques.name: Personification walked on stage
techniques.definition: An abstract idea given a body, a costume and lines to speak.
techniques.inThisBook: Revenge, Rape and Murder knock at Titus's study door in 5.2, which is what an old morality play would do in earnest. They are a queen and her two sons in costume, and Titus has already named her to her face by the evidence of his own stump, so the allegory is a lie both sides keep up until he cuts two of its throats.

techniques.name: Grief pushed past its limit
techniques.definition: Exaggeration held so long that it stops being ornament and becomes the state of the speaker.
techniques.inThisBook: Titus offers to water the earth until eternal spring grows on it, declares himself the sea and Lavinia the weeping sky, and says his sorrow has no bottom. Marcus keeps asking him to speak with possibility, and he cannot.

techniques.name: The set piece
techniques.definition: A long formal speech that halts the action and asks to be admired on its own terms.
techniques.inThisBook: Marcus's forty lines over the mutilated Lavinia at 2.4 stop the play dead. Lutes, conduits, Titan's face, Cerberus: the verse is exquisite and it leaves her standing there bleeding while he finishes.

techniques.name: Black comedy
techniques.definition: Jokes placed where an audience expects horror, so that laughter and disgust arrive together.
techniques.inThisBook: Titus laughs on hearing he has no tears left, Marcus explains that the fly resembled the empress's Moor, and a clown is hanged for delivering a letter with two pigeons. Productions discover the play is funny and then have to decide what to do about it.

quotations.text: Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods? Draw near them then in being merciful. Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge.
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Kneeling in the street, begging Titus to spare her eldest son Alarbus.
quotations.analysis: She argues in Rome's own vocabulary, and she argues well: nobility, the gods, mercy as a mark of rank. Titus answers with the word religiously and burns the boy anyway. Everything Tamora does for the rest of the play is licensed by the fact that she asked properly first and was refused on a technicality of rite.

quotations.text: O cruel, irreligious piety!
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: As her son is led off to be hacked apart and burned on the Andronici tomb.
quotations.analysis: Four words that hold the play's whole difficulty. Titus has just used the word religiously to justify the killing, and she hands it straight back with cruel attached. The line concedes that the sacrifice is genuinely pious and insists that piety is what makes it monstrous, which is the charge Rome never answers.

quotations.text: Thou art a Roman; be not barbarous.
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Kneeling with Titus's sons, begging him to let Mutius be buried in the family tomb.
quotations.analysis: Marcus means it as a compliment and the play hears it as a question. Roman and barbarous have been opposed since the first scene, where Chiron said Scythia was never half so barbarous as this. The distinction has already collapsed: the Roman thing and the barbarous thing were the same act, performed at the same tomb, an hour earlier.

quotations.text: These words are razors to my wounded heart.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: After Saturninus has sneered at Lavinia as a changing piece and at Titus's sons as lawless.
quotations.analysis: The first blade in a play full of them, and it is only a figure of speech. By Act III the metaphors have all come true: hands actually come off, tongues actually go, and the razor is a real knife held by a father over two bound men. Again and again Titus’s language predicts the stage business that arrives to replace it.

quotations.text: I'll find a day to massacre them all, And raze their faction and their family, The cruel father and his traitorous sons, To whom I sued for my dear son's life
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Aside to Saturninus, while publicly urging him to forgive Titus.
quotations.analysis: The double voice is the whole of her method: aloud she is reconciling the court, under her breath she is naming a date. Note what she lists as the grievance. Not the war, not the captivity, not the yoke; the refusal of a kneeling woman in the street. She is precise about the debt, and she collects on exactly that account.

quotations.text: Vengeance is in my heart, death in my hand, Blood and revenge are hammering in my head.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Refusing Tamora's invitation to lie down with her in the wood.
quotations.analysis: Tamora has just spent twenty lines on birds, shade and a golden slumber. Aaron cuts across her pastoral with three body parts and a verb from a forge. Hammering makes revenge a trade with tools and a rhythm, and it tells the audience who is actually running the plot: the man turning her down for a morning’s work, not the empress.

quotations.text: Hadst thou in person ne'er offended me, Even for his sake am I pitiless.
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Answering Lavinia, who has begged her in the name of Titus's mercy to Tamora herself.
quotations.analysis: Lavinia's argument is that Titus spared Tamora's life, so Tamora owes the daughter something. The reply concedes the debt and converts it: precisely because Titus is the father, the daughter is the payment. Hadst thou in person is the cruellest part. Tamora states outright that Lavinia has done nothing, and will suffer for that reason.

quotations.text: So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak, Who 'twas that cut thy tongue and ravished thee.
quotations.speaker: Demetrius
quotations.context: The first words of the scene, as the brothers leave Lavinia in the wood.
quotations.analysis: The play opens its most notorious scene with a taunt made out of the mechanics of the crime. Philomela in Ovid was silenced and still wove the truth; Demetrius thinks he has closed that loophole by taking the hands as well. The rest of the act, and most of the next two, is the play proving him wrong by a staff and a sandy plot.

quotations.text: Write down thy mind, bewray thy meaning so, An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
quotations.speaker: Chiron
quotations.context: Joining his brother's mockery before they leave her alone.
quotations.analysis: The play takes the joke literally: it becomes the instrument of his death. Two acts later Lavinia does play the scribe, guiding a staff with her stumps and her mouth, and writes his name. Chiron names the method by which he will be identified, bound, gagged and bled over a basin. Few taunts in Shakespeare are repaid so exactly.

quotations.text: Fair Philomela, why she but lost her tongue, And in a tedious sampler sewed her mind; But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Alone with Lavinia in the wood, in the middle of his forty-line speech over her.
quotations.analysis: The word but is doing terrible work here: Philomela only lost her tongue. Marcus reaches for a literary precedent and finds it insufficient, which is the most honest thing in the speech. The scene has divided readers for two centuries, because the verse is beautiful and a woman is bleeding through all of it while a man looks for the right comparison.

quotations.text: Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers? Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey But me and mine.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Telling his banished son that exile is good fortune.
quotations.analysis: Titus gave this city his sons, his arm and the empire, and here he sees it plainly for the first time. Wilderness is the sharp word: it means no Rome at all, a wood with animals in it, far worse than a corrupt Rome to be reformed. He has just come from the forest where his daughter was attacked, and he no longer distinguishes the two places.

quotations.text: Let fools do good, and fair men call for grace, Aaron will have his soul black like his face.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Leaving with Titus's severed hand, having just told the audience the sons are already dead.
quotations.analysis: He takes Rome's insult and makes it a rhyme and a policy. Fair men call for grace pins the hypocrisy: the same city that equates whiteness with virtue has just cheated an old man out of his hand. Aaron takes the identity Rome has assigned him and makes it his own, which is not the same as agreeing with it.

quotations.text: Why dost thou laugh? It fits not with this hour.
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Immediately after Titus responds to the arrival of his sons' heads with laughter.
quotations.analysis: Marcus speaks for the part of the audience still trying to keep the genre steady. Titus’s answer is that he has no tears left, which is accountancy, not madness: grief has a supply and it has run out. The laugh is the moment the play stops being a tragedy of suffering and becomes a tragedy of planning.

quotations.text: Thou shalt not sigh, nor hold thy stumps to heaven, Nor wink, nor nod, nor kneel, nor make a sign, But I of these will wrest an alphabet
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: At the family dinner, promising Lavinia that he will learn to read her.
quotations.analysis: The tenderest speech he makes, and it is also a claim of ownership over her meaning. Wrest is a violent verb for a loving promise: he will force a language out of her body whether the signs are offered or not. The play gives her a father who will not stop attending to her and never once asks her a question she could answer.

quotations.text: Pardon me, sir; 'twas a black ill-favoured fly, Like to the empress' Moor; therefore I killed him.
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Explaining himself after Titus has accused him of murder for swatting a fly at dinner.
quotations.analysis: Marcus invents the excuse on the spot and it works instantly: Titus takes the knife and stabs the dead fly twice more, once for Aaron and once for Tamora. The scene shows grief turning into method, and it shows the family's racism in its most casual form, offered as a joke to calm a distressed old man.

quotations.text: Stuprum. Chiron. Demetrius.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Reading aloud what Lavinia has written in the sand with a staff held in her mouth.
quotations.analysis: Three words, one of them Latin, and the play's only piece of direct testimony. Stuprum is the legal term, not a cry: she names the crime in the language of the courts that failed her, then names the men. After two acts of other people describing her, this is Lavinia speaking, and it takes a stick, a patch of sand and both her stumps.

quotations.text: Coal-black is better than another hue In that it scorns to bear another hue; For all the water in the ocean Can never turn the swan's black legs to white
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Defending his newborn son against Chiron, Demetrius and the nurse sent to kill it.
quotations.analysis: The argument is that black keeps its own colour and white cannot. Fifteen lines later Chiron says he blushes at the family shame, and Aaron pounces: a treacherous hue that betrays the counsels of the heart. It is the one speech in the play where blackness is a boast, made by a man holding a newborn in one arm and a scimitar in the other.

quotations.text: My mistress is my mistress; this my self; The vigour and the picture of my youth. This before all the world do I prefer; This maugre all the world will I keep safe
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Asked whether he will betray Tamora to protect the child.
quotations.analysis: He drops the empress in half a line and never mentions her again with any warmth. The repetition of this, three times, keeps pointing at the baby in his arms while the sentence gets shorter and harder. Aaron is the only character in the play who chooses a living child over an inherited quarrel, and he is the one buried alive for it.

quotations.text: And sith there's no justice in earth nor hell, We will solicit heaven and move the gods To send down Justice for to wreak our wrongs.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Handing out bows and arrows with letters tied to them, to be shot into the emperor's court.
quotations.analysis: He has already sent men to dig for Justice underground and to drag the sea for her. The logic is perfectly sound and the method is ridiculous, which is how this play does madness: a rational man following a failed system to its last address, with no confusion at all. The arrows land in the palace, and Saturninus reads them as libel.

quotations.text: But I have done a thousand dreadful things As willingly as one would kill a fly, And nothing grieves me heartily indeed But that I cannot do ten thousand more.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: On a ladder with a rope round his neck, having just listed his crimes to Lucius.
quotations.analysis: The comparison reaches back to Act III, where a killed fly reduced Titus to fury and then to knife-work. Aaron uses the same insect to measure indifference. He has bought his son's life with this confession and spends the rest of it refusing the remorse that would make the bargain look like repentance.

quotations.text: Know thou, sad man, I am not Tamora; She is thy enemy, and I thy friend. I am Revenge, sent from th' infernal kingdom
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: At the door of Titus's study, dressed as Revenge with her sons as Rape and Murder.
quotations.analysis: She thinks she is exploiting his madness and she is walking into his kitchen. Titus has already told her he knows her by his own stump, and he lets the disguise stand because it hands him her sons. The old morality figures knock at the door, the play lets them in, and then butchers two of them behind it.

quotations.text: Why, there they are, both baked in that pie, Whereof their mother daintily hath fed, Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Asked by Saturninus to fetch Chiron and Demetrius to the banquet.
quotations.analysis: The line is delivered as information, in answer to a polite request, by a man dressed as a cook. Daintily does the damage: it makes Tamora a guest with manners while she finishes her sons. Three lines later he stabs her, and the revenge that began with a boy burned on a tomb is settled over dinner in under thirty seconds.

quotations.text: I am no baby, I, that with base prayers I should repent the evils I have done. Ten thousand worse than ever yet I did Would I perform, if I might have my will. If one good deed in all my life I did, I do repent it from my very soul.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Sentenced by Lucius to be set breast-deep in earth and starved.
quotations.analysis: His last speech gives no sign of the scaffold conversion an Elizabethan audience expected and an Elizabethan gallows usually produced. The final couplet is a joke with a real fact inside it: he did do one good deed, and everyone on stage is looking at it, because the baby he saved is alive in Lucius's household while he goes into the ground.

quotations.text: O, let me teach you how to knit again This scattered corn into one mutual sheaf, These broken limbs again into one body
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Speaking down to the people of Rome from the upper stage, with four fresh bodies below.
quotations.analysis: The old civic language comes back for the ending: the state as a sheaf, the state as a body. Broken limbs is a metaphor that has been literal for three acts, and an audience that has watched hands and heads come off cannot hear it as figure any more. Marcus asks Rome to reassemble itself using the vocabulary that failed it.

timeline.label: Ovid completes the Metamorphoses
timeline.detail: Book VI tells of Tereus, Philomela and the weaving that exposes him, and of the meal Procne serves afterwards. Shakespeare puts the book itself on stage in Act IV.

timeline.label: Seneca His Tenne Tragedies printed in English
timeline.detail: Thomas Newton's collection put Thyestes and its banquet of children into the hands of English playwrights and their audiences.

timeline.label: Titus Andronicus written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to the early 1590s, and often called Shakespeare's first tragedy. Some arguments for an earlier start rest on Jonson's later joke about the play's ageing admirers.

timeline.label: Performed at the Rose on 24 January
timeline.detail: Philip Henslowe recorded the takings for Titus & ondronicus in his account book, marking it as a new play for Sussex's Men.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register and printed
timeline.detail: John Danter entered A Noble Roman Historye of Tytus Andronicus on 6 February and printed the quarto for Edward White and Thomas Millington. It is the first printing of any Shakespeare play, and one copy survives.

timeline.label: Second quarto
timeline.detail: James Roberts printed Q2 for Edward White; Edward Allde printed a third quarto for White in 1611. Both show the play still selling twenty years on.

timeline.label: Jonson jokes about it in Bartholomew Fair
timeline.detail: The Induction mocks playgoers who still call Titus Andronicus the best thing going, saying their judgement has stood still for twenty-five or thirty years.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed among the tragedies, from a copy of Q3 marked up against a playhouse manuscript. The Folio alone prints the fly scene at 3.2.

timeline.label: Ravenscroft's adaptation
timeline.detail: Edward Ravenscroft rewrote it as Titus Andronicus, or The Rape of Lavinia, and his preface began the long tradition of doubting that Shakespeare wrote all of it.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs Olivier and Vivien Leigh
timeline.detail: At Stratford, with stylised blood and Laurence Olivier as Titus. The production is generally credited with making the play stageable again after two centuries of embarrassment.

timeline.label: Deborah Warner at the Swan
timeline.detail: With Brian Cox as Titus, Estelle Kohler as Tamora and Sonia Ritter as Lavinia. The staging let the play be funny, and found that the laughter made the horror worse.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film Titus
timeline.detail: Anthony Hopkins and Jessica Lange, in a design that mixes Roman architecture with twentieth-century fascism. Harry Lennix's Aaron brought the part to a wide audience.

places.name: Rome
places.note: The Capitol, the Pantheon and the Andronici tomb. The play's Rome belongs to no datable reign, which leaves it a city of rites, elections and burials with no year attached.

places.name: The Rose, Bankside
places.note: Where Henslowe recorded a performance on 24 January 1594, the earliest firm evidence that the play was being acted.

places.name: Stationers' Hall, London
places.note: Where John Danter entered the play on 6 February 1594, two weeks after the Rose performance and just before printing it.

places.name: Folger Shakespeare Library, Washington
places.note: Holds the only surviving copy of the 1594 quarto, found in Sweden in 1904 and sold to Henry Clay Folger the year after.

places.name: Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon
places.note: Where Deborah Warner staged the play in 1987, in the production that settled its modern reputation.

criticalViews.position: George Peele wrote part of it
criticalViews.summary: Stylistic and statistical work, most insistently by Brian Vickers, assigns Act I, 2.1 and 4.1 to George Peele on the evidence of vocabulary, verse habits and a taste for classical roll-calls that thins out sharply after the first act.
criticalViews.counter: The tests disagree with each other about where the seams fall, and the scenes credited to Peele include the sacrifice of Alarbus, which every later act depends on. A collaborator who set up the whole machine is hard to distinguish from an author writing early.

criticalViews.position: Aaron is the play's clearest moral intelligence
criticalViews.summary: He sees Rome accurately when nobody else does, names the hypocrisy of fair men calling for grace, and is the only character who protects a child instead of avenging one. Readings since the 1980s have moved him out of the villain's slot and into the centre of the play.
criticalViews.counter: He also invents the pit, the letter and the severed-hand trick, and tells Lucius he wishes he had done ten thousand worse things. A reading that rescues him has to explain why the play gives him so much pleasure in the suffering we are also meant to condemn.

criticalViews.position: The play is about who is permitted to speak for a victim
criticalViews.summary: Lavinia is described, interpreted, wept over and finally killed, and the one time she testifies she has to do it with a stick in her teeth. Feminist criticism from the 1980s on has read the play as an exposure of how a woman's injury becomes everyone else's material.
criticalViews.counter: The exposure and the exploitation use the same forty lines. Marcus's speech is written to be admired, and a production that plays it for beauty reproduces the appropriation the reading objects to; one that plays it for embarrassment loses the verse the play actually wrote.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Titus responsible for what happens to his family?
essayQuestions.focus: Ritual, choice and consequence in Act I
plan: Start with the sacrifice of Alarbus at 1.1 and note that Lucius asks for it, Titus grants it, and Tamora argues against it in Rome's own terms and loses.
Follow the decisions of the rest of the scene: refusing the empire, giving it to Saturninus, killing Mutius, and then accepting Tamora's public reconciliation at face value.
Set Tamora's aside at 1.1.451 beside her answer to Lavinia at 2.3.161, and show that she names the refusal in the street as the exact debt she is collecting.
Weigh the counter-case: the trap at the pit, the forged letter and the bargain for his hand are Aaron's inventions, and Titus could not have foreseen any of them.
Close by asking what the fly scene at 3.2 shows about how much of his later method was in him from the first act.

essayQuestions.question: 'The play makes Lavinia's body do the work of speech.' Discuss.
plan: Establish that she speaks freely and sharply in 2.3, arguing with Tamora, so the silence that follows is something done to her and not a character trait.
Examine Marcus's speech at 2.4 in detail, including the word but at 2.4.38, and decide whether the verse attends to her or replaces her.
Read Titus's promise to wrest an alphabet at 3.2.42 as both devotion and a claim on her meaning.
Treat 4.1.79 as the turning point: Lavinia names the crime in legal Latin and the men in plain Roman letters, using a staff and her stumps.
Finish with her death at 5.3.46, where her father asks Saturninus for a precedent and kills her without asking her anything.

essayQuestions.question: What does Aaron contribute to the play beyond villainy?
essayQuestions.focus: Race, fatherhood and the limits of sympathy
plan: List what he actually engineers: the gold, the letter, the pit, the hand, the heads, and his own delight at the crack in the wall in 5.1.
Set against it the language Rome uses about him, from the nurse's loathsome as a toad to Lucius's incarnate devil, and note how much of it is about colour.
Work through 4.2, where he kills the nurse, defies Tamora and takes the child, and compare his defence of his son with Titus's treatment of Mutius and Lavinia.
Use 3.1.205 and 4.2.99 to show how he converts an imposed insult into a claim, and ask whether that is defiance or self-hatred taking a proud form.
End on 5.3.185 and the fact that the one good deed he repents is the child who is alive and safe while he is buried to the chest.

essayQuestions.question: Does the ending of Titus Andronicus restore order?
plan: Count what is settled in 5.3: four deaths in nine lines, an emperor acclaimed, burials assigned and a sentence passed on Aaron.
Read Marcus's sheaf-and-body speech at 5.3.70 and ask whether the civic vocabulary has earned its return after three acts in which limbs came off for real.
Test Lucius's credentials: he demanded the sacrifice in Act I, he returns with the army of the people whose prince he burned, and he swears by a god to a man who has none.
Look at the final orders, which reward and punish through burial, and note that this is precisely the currency the play opened with.
Decide what the last two lines about the birds do to the ending's claim to have finished with cruelty.

discussionQuestions: Tamora asks for mercy in Rome's own language and is refused on a point of rite. Is Titus wrong at 1.1, or only unlucky?
Marcus's forty lines over Lavinia are some of the finest verse in the play. Should a production let them be beautiful?
Titus laughs when the heads arrive. What has to have happened to a person for that to be the response?
Aaron saves his son and regrets nothing else. Does that one act change how you read everything he does before it?
Chiron jeers that Lavinia should write with her stumps, and two acts later she does. Is the play satisfying here, or merely neat?
Lucius ends the play as emperor, having asked for the sacrifice that started it. What sort of Rome has he inherited?

related.why: The play names Lucrece three times and swears its revenge oath on Brutus's example; the poem is the story Titus and Marcus keep reaching for when they need a precedent.
The other Shakespeare revenge play, with the same machinery of feigned madness, a delayed reckoning and a court that cannot be told the truth directly.
Shakespeare's other Roman tragedy of a general the city honours and then cannot live with, ending again with a soldier leading an enemy army home.
The later play that puts a black man at the centre of the tragedy, and lets the audience hear how Venice talks about him when it thinks he is not listening.
Webster takes up the same stagecraft of horror as spectacle, including a scene of body parts presented to a grieving relative as a message.
